summary: This work develops a systematic frequency-collision analysis for cross-resonance gates in the far-detuned regime ($3\alpha_c \le \Delta_{ct} \le \alpha_c$) of fixed-frequency transmon processors, showing that this regime significantly improves tolerance to fabrication-induced qubit-frequency spread compared to the conventional straddling regime. Using a long-time-averaged numerical method to accurately model high-intensity smoothly-ramped drives, the authors derive collision-free conditions, perform frequency-allocation optimization via linear programming, and demonstrate that 1024-qubit square-lattice devices require only $\sigma_f/2\pi \le 6.8$ MHz for 10% collision-free yield at 0.1% error threshold—approximately twofold better than current achievable spread.
motivation: Frequency crowding severely limits scaling of fixed-frequency transmon processors because the straddling regime ($0 \le \Delta_{ct} \le -\alpha_c$) constrains qubit frequencies to a narrow range, making systems highly susceptible to frequency collisions that degrade gate fidelity. Current straddling designs achieve vanishing collision-free yields at thousand-qubit scales even with modest error budgets.
method: A five-step framework combining: (1) extraction of three-qubit chains from lattices; (2) numerical two-dimensional collision-landscape sweeps incorporating smooth pulse ramps via long-time-averaged transition probabilities; (3) identification of collision processes and extraction of collision windows; (4) max–min linear-programming optimization of frequency allocations on 4×4 unit cells with periodic boundary conditions; and (5) Monte Carlo yield estimation for 1024-qubit devices under realistic Gaussian qubit-frequency spread.
result: Far-detuned CR designs require $\sigma_{10\%}/2\pi = 6.8$ MHz (square), 8.9 MHz (hexagonal), and 12.9 MHz (heavy-hexagonal) for 10% collision-free yield on 1024-qubit devices at 0.1% error threshold, compared to 0.1, 1.4, and 2.1 MHz respectively for straddling designs—an order-of-magnitude improvement, requiring approximately 2× reduction from state-of-the-art $\sigma_f/2\pi \approx 14.5$ MHz to reach feasibility.
